name: Jamal Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Dr Wagner. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Jamal, please. I work at Brookfield Health Centre, which serves a big new housing estate on the edge of the city, mostly young families and commuters. I do morning clinic, a block of phone and video appointments after lunch, and then I sort the results inbox, which is the bit everyone hates. I'm one year qualified and still the slowest doctor there, but I'm the one they call when the computer system crashes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the babies and the new parents, honestly, the six-week checks are the best part of my week. I use AI every day: I draft my referral letters with it, I use it to check interactions between drugs, and on Saturdays I get paid by a small health app company to check whether their symptom checker gives safe advice. What wears me out is money, oddly, because I share a flat with my friend Theo, a software tester, and between rent, my student loan and my car, I've got maybe two weeks of savings. The Saturday work pays about £300 a month and that's what keeps us afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be surprised, given what I already use it for, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, not magic, and I'd say that's exactly what I've been telling people for a year. At work I'd keep showing colleagues the few tricks that save time. Online I'd probably write a short post about which bits actually work in a clinic, because there's so much hype on both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd hit my side income first. If the bubble bursts, small health app companies like the one I check for go bust, and that's £300 a month I rely on. My doctor's job is fine. The extra £300 a month from the health app company is what's fragile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brookfield and keep using the tools that work. I'd look for a second Saturday client now, before the first one folds, maybe a medical publisher that needs doctors to check content. And I'd move £100 a month into savings until I have two months, which means fewer weekends away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight, mostly about the money. Not about the career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely do you think it is that your Saturday work dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, fairly likely. The app company is twelve people in a shared office and they live on investors' money, and investors leave when the hype dies. I'd give it a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the £300 went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. I could get the bus to Brookfield, it's forty minutes instead of fifteen. Theo would say cut the takeaways, but the takeaways are what keep me sane after a Thursday clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels like where we're heading, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's use it properly, and let's measure whether patients are better off. At work I'd volunteer to set up whatever the health centre buys. I'd also say, publicly, that we shouldn't let it make the clinic feel like a call centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. I'm already the person who knows the tools, and the thinking tasks that go first are the ones I already hand to AI. The danger is that clinics hire fewer juniors, but I'd make myself useful in a way that's hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead the setup of an AI triage system at Brookfield, the kind that sorts the morning phone calls by urgency, and ask for one paid session a week for it. I'd push the app company to give me more hours, because in this world they'd grow. And I'd do a short course on medical device safety rules, so I actually understand the regulations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous for the people around me, less for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be nervous for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo, my flatmate, more than anyone. Software testing is exactly the kind of checking work on the card. If my flatmate Theo loses his software testing job, the rent on our flat lands on me, and two weeks of savings doesn't cover that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this is good for you, but your rent depends on Theo's job. Is it still good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my career, yes. For the flat, less so. I'd probably tell Theo to start looking now, and I'd quietly look at one-bed flats closer to the health centre, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Okay, that changes the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need honest, fast planning from the government and the health service. I'd say it publicly, I'd probably go on a podcast if someone asked. I'd also say doctors who refuse to engage will be left behind, which wouldn't make me popular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my thinking work is gone by 2028, and the clinic keeps a few experienced doctors for the hands-on part until the robots in 2031. I'm junior, so that's not me. But the companies building these systems will need doctors to test them and take legal responsibility, and I'd be one of the few young doctors who already does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd ask the health app company for a full-time clinical safety job, or apply to a bigger one in the city. I'd keep a couple of sessions a week at Brookfield, doing baby checks and examinations, because that's hands-on and stays human for a few years. And I'd move into the city if the job was there, maybe into a shared house to keep rent down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but awake. Like the first night on call, when you're scared but also oddly alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose if you left most of your clinic work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The six-week baby checks, mainly. There's a mum on the estate who brought her twins to me and then her own mum, and I'd miss being that family's doctor. But I'd rather have a job than be a sentimental doctor with no income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say she didn't raise a doctor to work for a tech company. I'd tell her I'm still a doctor, I'm just checking the machine that does the first part. She wouldn't buy it at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to set things up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if we start now, and I'd say that to anyone at work who's burying their head. I'd say the health service should train every doctor on these tools by 2028. Online, I'd keep sharing what works and what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in a good position. By 2031 I'd be a fully trained family doctor with five years of experience using these tools, which would be rare. The thinking work changes on schedule, but I'd be one of the people steering it rather than being steered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training by 2029 and keep the Saturday work. I'd start putting £50 a month into a cheap index fund, which is just a basket of many company shares, because if AI makes money I'd like a tiny bit of it. And I'd apply for a health informatics fellowship around 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. Focused. The money's still thin, but I'd feel ahead of the curve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting money into shares with two weeks of savings. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, honestly. I'd build a month of savings first, then start the £50. I'm comfortable with risk, but I'm not stupid about it. I've seen what happens when the car breaks down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Theo in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to retrain, maybe into security testing, which he's been talking about. I'd push him to start now. We'd keep the flat for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career's worth of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and doctors who use it will be fine. At work I'd be the one running lunchtime sessions on the tools. Publicly I'd keep it balanced, because people get tired of evangelists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best picture for me. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, experienced in medicine and in AI, and the robots don't arrive until 2039. I'd probably end up leading AI work for a group of clinics, which is exactly what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, take the informatics fellowship, and stay at Brookfield part-time so I don't lose touch with patients. I'd build savings to three months, then invest a bit every month. And I'd run monthly lunchtime sessions on the AI tools for the other doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that ten years makes people lazy. If everyone thinks there's loads of time, nobody plans, and then it's 2034 and the panic starts. I'd worry about colleagues sleepwalking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a patient who asked about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that in ten years they might see an AI first, and a doctor second, and that the doctor will still be the one who listens. I believe that, mostly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's too fast for my savings, even if I'd land somewhere eventually. What would help is paid time to move into the new roles, and the health service hiring doctors to test and supervise the AI instead of leaving it to the companies. And honestly, a month's pay as a buffer for juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who's checking the machines. Right now, a lot of the checking of medical AI is done by people like me on a Saturday, paid by the hour. That's not good enough for something that will see millions of patients.
